stories.headline: Twelve Killed as Bus Carrying Polish Pilgrims Veers Off Hungarian Motorway
stories.summary:
A bus carrying Polish pilgrims from the Podkarpacie region overturned in the early hours of Sunday after leaving the M3 motorway in Hungary, killing twelve people and injuring dozens more. Police believe the driver fell asleep at the wheel; he has been taken into custody and questioned. The bus, which had been returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina, carried 57 passengers and two drivers, with 35 people rescued by firefighters as of Sunday morning.

Hungary's ambulance service reported treating one person with life-threatening injuries, nine with serious injuries, and 37 with minor injuries. Emergency crews worked to lift the 24-tonne bus with cranes after struggling to reach people trapped beneath the rear axle. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar offered condolences to victims' families.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had dispatched a special aircraft carrying foreign ministry officials and medical personnel to the scene. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed that Hungarian police had already begun questioning the bus driver. The crash is one of the deadliest road accidents in Central Europe this year.

stories.headline: Michigan Democrat Stevens Urges Senate Candidate El-Sayed to Cut Ties with Streamer Hasan Piker
stories.summary:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) said Sunday it "certainly makes sense" for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to sever his affiliation with popular left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary, made the comments on Fox News's "The Sunday Briefing," reflecting broader concerns within the Democratic Party about whether progressive candidates aligned with hard-left influencers can perform in competitive general elections.

El-Sayed, a progressive backed by prominent left-wing figures, now faces Republican Mike Rogers in a general election contest for Michigan's open Senate seat, a race viewed as potentially pivotal in the battle for Senate control. Piker has drawn controversy for past remarks that critics say are politically toxic in swing-state terrain. Gun-control activist Shannon Watts also publicly clashed with Piker over Democrats' responsibility for political rhetoric.

The episode highlights an ongoing tension within the Democratic Party between its progressive base and more moderate factions over candidate positioning ahead of the midterms. Analysts have noted that candidates closely aligned with activist-left figures have historically underperformed in competitive districts, and the Michigan Senate race is considered a key battleground.

stories.headline: California Billionaire Tax Heads to November Ballot as Mark Cuban Warns of Investment Exodus
stories.summary:
California voters will decide this November on a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on state residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion, retroactive to January 1, 2026. The measure, backed by the Service Employees International Union, is projected to generate billions of dollars for healthcare and education, according to supporters. The initiative has ignited a high-profile public debate about whether high-tax policies accelerate the departure of wealthy residents and investment from the state.

Billionaire investor Mark Cuban warned Saturday that the tax could drive not only wealthy individuals out of California but also startups and the investors who back them, threatening the state's innovation economy. Cuban's comments came amid a public exchange with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, who has defended the measure as a necessary tool for funding public services. Cuban said he would steer future investments away from California if the tax passes.

IRS data cited in the debate show significant net taxpayer outflows from California counties in recent years, with Los Angeles County alone recording a net loss of 17,496 tax filers and nearly $1.9 billion in income to other states. Governor Gavin Newsom has publicly opposed the state-level billionaire tax while separately advocating for a similar measure at the federal level. Supporters contend that wealth concentration in the state is so extreme that the tax would have a minimal effect on residency decisions while generating substantial public revenue.

stories.headline: Ferrari's First Electric Car Sells for Record $40 Million at Charity Auction
stories.summary:
Ferrari's first all-electric production car, the Luce, fetched $40 million at a Sotheby's charity auction in California on Sunday, setting a record for a new car sold at auction and exceeding the vehicle's standard price by more than 35 times. The auctioned model featured a bespoke white finish, custom wheels, and specialized brakes. All proceeds will be donated to the Ferrari Foundation's educational programs.

The Luce, designed by former Apple chief design officer Sir Jony Ive, generated significant controversy when it launched in May, with critics — including Ferrari's former chairman Luca Cordero di Montezemolo and Italy's Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini — arguing it departed too sharply from the brand's motorsport heritage. Ferrari shares fell the day after its unveiling. The car is a five-seat, battery-powered vehicle, a significant departure from the brand's traditional lineup.

Despite the backlash, Sunday's record-setting sale underscores intense collector demand for the marque's historic firsts. A bespoke Daytona SP3 previously set the prior record for a new Ferrari at auction, raising $26 million in 2025. The sale arrives as Ferrari and other European automakers work to compete in the electric vehicle market increasingly dominated by Tesla and Chinese manufacturers.

stories.headline: Update: Kushner Meets Hamas Leadership in Egypt in Push to Revive Gaza Ceasefire
stories.summary:
Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and envoy, held a rare 90-minute meeting Sunday with Hamas's political leadership in Egypt, pressing the group to take concrete steps toward disarmament under the U.S.-backed 15-point peace road map. A source with direct knowledge described the meeting as "very productive," with Hamas leaders reaffirming their commitment to disarm and demilitarize Gaza. Kushner is scheduled to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday to continue the diplomatic push.

The talks come one week after Netanyahu publicly rejected the Trump administration's latest Gaza peace proposal, creating a significant rupture in U.S.-Israel negotiations. The Trump administration has characterized Netanyahu's rejection as campaign rhetoric ahead of Israeli elections, and officials say they remain committed to the road map. Hamas, following the meeting, called on the U.S.-led Board of Peace to compel Israel to accept the plan.

The diplomatic flurry represents a new and unusual direct engagement between a senior U.S. official and Hamas leadership, a group the United States designates as a terrorist organization. The meetings signal the Trump administration's determination to advance a resolution even as both parties to the conflict have resisted key elements of the proposal. The outcome of Kushner's Monday meeting with Netanyahu will be closely watched as a measure of whether the road map can survive.

stories.headline: Update: Indonesia Earthquake Death Toll Reaches 53 as 5,000 Displaced, Rescue Efforts Continue
stories.summary:
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck the Indonesian island of Flores in the early hours of Saturday has killed at least 53 people and displaced approximately 5,000, with rescue operations still ongoing as authorities work to reach remote and mountainous areas. The shallow quake, occurring just 15 kilometers below the surface, triggered 341 aftershocks and a subsequent magnitude 6.9 tremor elsewhere in the country, compounding the disaster.

More than 900 homes and hundreds of other buildings, including schools, healthcare facilities, and government offices, were severely damaged. Ruteng Regional Hospital in Manggarai province suffered ceiling collapses, forcing patients to be treated in tents. A hospital spokesperson said medical assistance had not yet arrived as of Sunday, though Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency said tonnes of emergency supplies had been dispatched.

The disaster is Indonesia's deadliest earthquake since 2022, when hundreds were killed in West Java. Officials say the full scale of destruction remains unclear given the region's difficult terrain. The Indonesian government has declared an emergency response, with meeting evacuees' basic needs identified as the top priority.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Orders Pentagon to Scale Back U.S.-South Korea Military Exercises, Citing Kim Relationship and Seoul's Refusal to Aid Iran War
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Sunday that he has directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" the upcoming Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises with South Korea, citing the cost of the drills and what he called an inappropriate and hostile signal to North Korea. Trump wrote on Truth Social that he has a "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and that North Korea has been "unthreatening and respectful" during his administration.

Trump also explicitly linked the decision to South Korea's refusal to support U.S. military operations against Iran, saying Seoul had declined his request to help denuclearize Iran. The move marks a significant shift in U.S. alliance posture on the Korean Peninsula and follows a pattern of Trump using longstanding alliance commitments as leverage in broader diplomatic disputes.

The decision drew immediate attention from defense analysts and lawmakers, with some Republicans and Democrats alike raising concerns about the message sent to both South Korea and North Korea at a time of heightened regional tensions. The exercises, which had been scheduled to begin this week, are considered a cornerstone of the U.S.-South Korea mutual defense treaty. South Korea has not yet issued a formal public response.

stories.headline: Liechtenstein Adopts Absolute Primogeniture, Opening Throne to Women for First Time
stories.summary:
Liechtenstein announced on its national day Sunday that it has changed its royal succession rules from male primogeniture to absolute primogeniture, meaning the throne will in future pass to the first-born child regardless of sex. The change was declared by the House of Liechtenstein, whose current ruler, Prince Hans-Adam II, has reigned since 1989.

The rule change will not affect the current succession line — Hereditary Prince Alois, Hans-Adam II's first-born son, remains the heir — but will apply to the descendants of Alois and his wife, Hereditary Princess Sophie. Alois said the change was made to ensure the principality is "led by the person who has been best prepared for this responsibility."

Liechtenstein, a landlocked microstate of roughly 44,000 people between Switzerland and Austria, is one of the few remaining European monarchies where the ruler retains sweeping political powers. The change mirrors reforms adopted by Britain in 2011. It marks a significant modernization of one of Europe's most traditional royal houses.

stories.headline: Attorney General Blanche Declines to Pledge DOJ Independence from Trump
stories.summary:
Attorney General Todd Blanche said Sunday he would not commit to acting independently of President Trump, telling NBC's Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, 'No, I'm not going to pledge that. And no attorney general should ever pledge that.' Blanche added that he would consider Trump's views when making decisions about individual prosecutions, while claiming the president has not and will not ask him to prosecute specific individuals.

The remarks drew immediate reaction across the political spectrum. Democrats framed Blanche's comments as confirmation that the Justice Department has been subordinated to the White House, pointing to Trump's earlier ouster of career DOJ staff and his public calls for investigations of political rivals. Supporters of the administration argued the attorney general serves at the president's direction and that Blanche's candor reflects how executive power has always functioned.

Blanche also addressed a recent DOJ opinion expanding executive privilege to cover communications between the president and private advisers outside the government, dismissing criticism of it as not raising 'any novel legal concept.' Critics have argued the opinion further insulates the White House from legal accountability.

The comments mark a significant public articulation of the Trump DOJ's operating philosophy heading into midterm elections, with implications for pending and potential federal investigations. Seven major outlets covered the interview, making it one of the most widely reported political stories of the day.

stories.headline: Republican Sen. Cassidy Accuses RFK Jr. of Breaking Pledge on Childhood Vaccine Schedule
stories.summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a physician, said Sunday that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. broke a pledge not to alter the childhood vaccine schedule, following President Trump's recent executive order directing changes to it. Appearing on ABC News's 'This Week,' Cassidy called the order 'a stupid thing to do' and said Trump's claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine were 'crazy' and damaging to public trust in immunization.

Cassidy said the practical effect of the order would require children to receive more individual shots rather than combined vaccines, telling host Martha Raddatz, 'Now instead of your child getting two shots, she has to get six shots.' He said Kennedy had provided 'guarantees' during his confirmation process that he would not attempt to alter the schedule, guarantees Cassidy said have now been broken.

The controversy places Cassidy — who voted to confirm Kennedy — in direct conflict with the administration on a public health matter with consequences for millions of American children and families. Supporters of the executive order argue that reviewing the vaccine schedule is a legitimate exercise of executive authority and that scrutiny of individual vaccine combinations is warranted.

The story is covered by four major outlets and represents a significant intraparty break, with a senior Republican senator publicly rebuking both the president and a cabinet secretary he helped confirm on a policy affecting nationwide childhood health standards.

stories.headline: Tommy John, Pioneering Baseball Pitcher and Namesake of Career-Saving Surgery, Dies at 83
stories.summary:
Tommy John, the left-handed MLB pitcher whose 1974 ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction became one of the most consequential surgeries in sports medicine history, died Sunday at his home in Florida at age 83. He was surrounded by his family, including his wife Cheryl, and had recently entered hospice care.

John was 31 years old when he tore the UCL in his pitching elbow — an injury that had effectively ended the careers of pitchers before him. He agreed to undergo an experimental procedure performed by surgeon Frank Jobe, returned to the mound, and went on to pitch for more than a decade afterward. The surgery that bears his name has since become routine, saving the careers of hundreds of professional and amateur pitchers.

A four-time All-Star, John played for six major league teams over a 26-year career. His willingness to undergo the risky, unproven surgery at a career crossroads is widely credited with transforming how arm injuries are treated across all levels of baseball and, increasingly, other sports.

The New York Yankees paid tribute to John on Sunday. He is remembered as much for that singular medical decision as for his playing career, having lent his name to a procedure that has become a permanent fixture of sports medicine.

stories.headline: Two Dead as Wildfires Force Evacuations on Greek Island of Salamina Near Athens
stories.summary:
Two people have died and approximately 90 residents have been evacuated by sea after two fires broke out within minutes of each other on Salamina, a Greek island of roughly 37,000 people situated just west of Athens. Fire officials deployed nearly 200 firefighters, five coastguard patrol boats, multiple aircraft, and 50 fire engines to contain the blazes, which spread rapidly due to high winds on a day the island was already under a high wildfire risk alert.

Authorities are working to prevent the two separate fires from merging into a single major wildfire by keeping the flames from cresting a mountain that divides the burn zones. Several private vessels are also assisting with the sea evacuation. The island has a notably elderly population, complicating evacuation efforts.

The Salamina fires are part of a broader pattern of extreme wildfire activity across Europe this weekend, driven by record heat. Croatia and Belgium have also seen significant wildfire evacuations and injuries in recent days. Greece has faced recurring devastating fire seasons in recent years, and the clustering of simultaneous ignitions has raised arson concerns among local officials, though no determination has been made.

stories.headline: Update: Supreme Court Emergency Docket Surges With Trump Requests on Mail Ballots and White House Construction
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court's emergency docket has seen a sharp surge in activity during the justices' summer recess, with the Trump administration pressing the court on two significant fronts: reviving presidential restrictions on mail-in ballots and allowing construction of a White House ballroom to resume after lower courts blocked both. The flurry of emergency applications again places the high court at the center of contentious political disputes during an election-sensitive period ahead of the November midterms.

Attorney General Todd Blanche separately indicated in a Sunday television appearance that the Justice Department may also seek Supreme Court intervention in the administration's efforts to compel states to turn over voter rolls to federal authorities. Blanche declined on NBC's Meet the Press to commit that the Justice Department would always act independently of the White House, saying, "No, I'm not going to pledge that. And no attorney general should ever pledge that."

Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and civil liberties groups, argue the administration is weaponizing the emergency docket to bypass normal judicial review on politically charged election-law questions ahead of the midterms. Supporters of the administration contend the restrictions are lawful exercises of executive authority over federal elections and federal property. The court's willingness to act on the requests during recess will be closely watched as a signal of how far the justices are prepared to go in adjudicating Trump administration emergency applications.

stories.headline: Update: Teenager Arrested in Virginia State University Shooting That Injured Five
stories.summary:
Camron Harris, a 19-year-old from Henrico, Virginia, was arrested after being found hiding in a campus closet following a shooting that injured five people outside a residence hall at Virginia State University in the early hours of Saturday. Harris is not a student at the university; only one of the five victims is enrolled there. A 21-year-old man remains in critical condition, while four others aged 17 to 23 sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

The arrest resolves an earlier uncertainty about the number of suspects: local police had initially told reporters they believed more than one shooter was involved, but the arrest of Harris appears to be the primary development. VSU, a historically Black university south of Richmond with more than 5,000 students, had just opened dormitories for the new semester when the shooting occurred.

The incident follows a separate shooting on the same day at a Lexington, Kentucky park concert that killed one person and injured four others, including two children. The back-to-back events prompted Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear to call for electing Democrats who would act on gun policy, illustrating the familiar partisan divide that follows mass shooting events in the United States.

stories.headline: McConnell Absence Deepens: Beshear Says Senator Has Not Responded, Calls for Public Accounting
stories.summary:
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear on Sunday publicly stated that Sen. Mitch McConnell has not responded to his requests for communication, intensifying scrutiny over the 84-year-old Republican senator's prolonged absence from public life. McConnell was hospitalized June 14 after a fall and has been in rehabilitation, with his office releasing only limited updates. He was discharged from a rehabilitation facility earlier this month and is receiving physical therapy at home, but has made no public appearances or direct statements to constituents.

"His boss are the people of Kentucky," Beshear said on CBS News' Face the Nation. "All he needs to do is call into this show for two minutes, or Fox News for two minutes, or do a video for two minutes to the people he's supposed to serve." Beshear, a Democrat, has previously written to McConnell demanding proof of his capacity to serve or his resignation, and has sent a copy to Senate Majority Leader John Thune urging an investigation.

McConnell's ongoing absence is having concrete legislative consequences: Republican leaders have cited his absence as a factor complicating efforts to advance the farm bill before the August recess. Senate Republicans have largely declined to comment publicly on McConnell's condition or capacity, with Beshear accusing GOP leadership of failing to hold itself accountable. McConnell's office has not responded to Beshear's latest public statements.

stories.headline: Eleven Killed in Israeli Strikes on Southern Lebanon in One of Deadliest Days Since June Agreement
stories.summary:
Israeli airstrikes killed at least eleven people in southern Lebanon on Saturday, making it one of the deadliest single days of attacks since a June agreement aimed at reducing hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said seven people — including three children and two women — were killed in a pre-dawn strike on a house on the outskirts of Ansar, roughly 70 kilometers south of Beirut. A second round of strikes later hit the town of Deir al-Zahrani, killing four more and wounding five others.

The Israel Defense Forces said the Ansar strike targeted Ali Samir al-Haj Hassan, described as a Hezbollah battalion commander in the elite Radwan Force unit, after a Hezbollah attack that seriously injured three Israeli soldiers. The IDF said Hassan had used his family and surrounding civilians as human shields inside a military headquarters, and that Israel did not learn until afterward that civilians were present in the compound. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office defended the strike on those grounds.

Lebanon and Hezbollah flatly rejected that account. Prime Minister Salam condemned the attacks as targeting civilians, not military infrastructure, and called on Israel to halt its escalation. Hezbollah accused Israel of deliberately targeting civilians in their homes and fabricating the military-site justification after the fact.

The strikes represent a significant flare-up along a front that has remained volatile despite the June de-escalation framework. The deaths drew immediate condemnation from Lebanese authorities and are likely to intensify international pressure on both sides, particularly given the involvement of Iran-backed Hezbollah and ongoing regional tensions following the broader U.S.-Iran conflict that drew Lebanon into the war in March.

stories.headline: Indiana Flooding Kills Five, Triggers Presidential Emergency Declaration as White River Inundates Indianapolis
stories.summary:
At least five people have died across Indiana as severe storms and flooding battered the state over the past week, with rescue operations continuing Saturday along the rising White River in Indianapolis. The Indianapolis Fire Department reported 95 people and 45 pets rescued by boat as of late afternoon, with dispatchers fielding hundreds of calls for service. Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett described the flooding as the city's worst in more than 30 years.

More than a dozen Indiana counties have declared local disasters, with damage concentrated along river corridors from Hamilton County into northern Indianapolis suburbs. Hundreds of homes between the river and parallel canals were evacuated Saturday, and a senior mobile home community in Tipton County and neighborhoods in Delaware and Fayette counties were also being cleared. Among the confirmed dead are a boy killed when a tree struck his home, a woman swept away after driving into floodwaters, and a teenager who went missing after jumping into a river.

President Trump approved a federal emergency declaration for Indiana, unlocking FEMA disaster assistance for the state. Conditions remained rapidly shifting Saturday, with river levels at record highs in multiple locations and forecasters warning that additional rainfall could further complicate rescue efforts.

stories.headline: Australia's New South Wales to Launch Gun Buyback After Bondi Beach Terror Attack
stories.summary:
New South Wales, Australia's most populous state, announced Saturday it will launch a gun buyback program beginning November 2, becoming the first Australian state to offer cash compensation for firearms in the wake of last December's Bondi Beach terror attack. Gun owners will be offered up to AUS$1,000 for eligible handguns, shotguns and rifles, with Premier Chris Minns saying the scheme could result in hundreds of thousands of weapons being surrendered.

The buyback follows sweeping firearm law reforms enacted after 15 people — including a 10-year-old girl and a Holocaust survivor — were killed at a Jewish festival on Bondi Beach on December 14. Under the new rules, individuals may own a maximum of four firearms, with exceptions for farmers and sports shooters capped at ten. The buyback targets those who now exceed those limits or no longer qualify under tightened licensing terms.

The scheme will operate in two phases: the first from November covering handguns, shotguns and rifles, and a second phase beginning early next year covering higher-value firearms worth above AUS$3,000, capped at AUS$10,000 in compensation. Businesses affected by the reforms are eligible for up to AUS$25,000 in adjustment support. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the move was essential to prevent a repeat of what he called an antisemitic terrorist attack.

stories.headline: Four Rare Renaissance Paintings Stolen from Museum in Sicily
stories.summary:
Four Renaissance paintings of what Italy's culture minister described as "extraordinary value" were stolen late Saturday from the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina in Sicily. The works — three panels of the Polyptych of San Gregorio and a double-sided panel of the Madonna with Child and Christ in Pietà — are all attributed to 15th-century Sicilian master Antonello da Messina, one of the defining painters of the early Renaissance.

Thieves entered the museum at approximately 9:50 p.m. local time and removed the paintings without triggering security alarms, according to police, who are investigating how the breach occurred and whether the theft was carried out by organized black-market art criminals working to order. One panel was extracted directly from inside a locked display case. Museum director Marisa Mercurio called it "a great loss for the museum, for the city, the community and the art world."

The theft is the latest in a series of high-profile museum heists across Europe, following a robbery at a museum near Parma earlier this year in which Cézanne, Renoir and and Matisse works worth €9 million were taken, and a brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris last year that netted €88 million in historic jewelry. Italian police have recovered the Parma paintings but the Sicilian works remain missing. Messina's mayor condemned the theft as a "heinous criminal act" against the heritage of the city.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Kills Five in Strikes Across Ukraine; Kyiv Launches Massive Drone Assault on Moscow
stories.summary:
At least five people were killed and more than ten injured across Ukraine as Russia launched a fresh wave of aerial attacks Saturday, striking 13 regions with ballistic missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said civilian infrastructure was targeted, including a book market in Kyiv's Pochayna district and a steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, where one man was found dead in rubble. Two people in their 60s were killed when a house was destroyed in Zaporizhzhia, and another person died in Sumy.

In a significant escalatory exchange, Ukraine launched approximately 600 drones toward Moscow overnight, according to the city's mayor. A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was struck and caught fire near the capital. Russia's defense ministry said 822 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, but at least seven people died across Russian regions from the strikes.

Russia claimed its attacks on Kyiv targeted a facility producing parts for Ukrainian Flamingo missiles and a drone component factory. Moscow also said it struck a steelworks in Kryvyi Rih it described as a weapons manufacturing site and hit a cargo vessel near Odesa it claimed was carrying military equipment. Ukraine has been stepping up attacks on Russian logistics hubs in recent weeks to disrupt military supplies.

A separate development drew international concern as a Ukrainian drone was reported downed in Romania, the latest in a series of drone incursion incidents in NATO airspace — raising questions about spillover risk as both sides dramatically escalate the tempo and scale of long-range strikes.

stories.headline: Update: Senate Panel Votes to Hold Fauci in Contempt After He Invokes Fifth Amendment 111 Times; Refuses Second Hearing
stories.summary:
A Senate committee voted along party lines last week to hold former NIAID Director Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 111 times during a July 29 hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. On Friday, Fauci declined a separate request to appear before Sen. Ron Johnson's Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, with his attorney arguing a second compelled appearance would amount to politically motivated harassment.

Committee chairman Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is seeking to send the contempt referral directly to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., bypassing a full Senate vote. At the legal center of the dispute is whether Fauci can validly invoke the Fifth Amendment given that former President Joe Biden issued him a preemptive pardon before leaving office. Paul has argued the pardon eliminates Fauci's risk of federal prosecution and therefore eliminates the constitutional basis for his refusal to answer questions; Fauci's attorneys dispute that interpretation.

Republicans on the committee are investigating Fauci's role in the federal government's COVID-19 response, including the safety and efficacy of vaccines, and allegations that he funded research that may have contributed to a lab leak of the virus in China — claims Fauci has repeatedly denied. The HHS has been ordered to hand over work iPhone records, and state-level subpoenas have been issued by officials in Florida, Alabama, and Louisiana following the contempt vote.

Democrats and Fauci's supporters have characterized the investigation as a politically driven witch hunt against a public health official who spent decades in government service. The contempt referral, if acted upon by the Justice Department, could set a significant legal precedent regarding the interplay between presidential pardons and congressional oversight powers.

stories.headline: Taliban Marks Five Years in Power at Loya Jirga as UN Warns of Grave Human Rights Crisis
stories.summary:
Taliban rulers and thousands of delegates gathered at Afghanistan's traditional Loya Jirga assembly hall in Kabul on Saturday to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to power following the U.S. and NATO withdrawal on August 15, 2021. Senior officials delivered speeches framing Taliban rule as Afghanistan's liberation from foreign occupation, with Deputy Prime Minister Abdul Salam Hanafi declaring an end to external interventions and internal strife. Some foreign representatives attended the ceremony alongside ordinary citizens.

A top United Nations official issued a stark counter-narrative, warning of a grave and worsening human rights crisis in the country. Since seizing power, the Taliban has banned girls from attending school beyond the sixth grade, prohibited women from universities, barred women from public spaces including gyms and parks, and restricted women from traveling without a male guardian — reversing pledges made before the takeover that women would have access to education, employment, and public life.

The five-year milestone comes as international recognition of the Taliban government remains essentially nonexistent, with no country having formally recognized the administration. Taliban officials detained six staff members of an Afghan women's rights group and several UN employees earlier in August, drawing international condemnation. The anniversary underscores the enduring consequences of the 2021 withdrawal, which triggered chaotic scenes at Kabul's airport as tens of thousands of Afghans attempted to flee.

stories.headline: Update: Alaska Senate Race Tightens as Peltola Distances Herself from Harris Endorsement
stories.summary:
Alaska's U.S. Senate race is emerging as an unexpected competitive contest heading into the November midterms, with Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan facing a serious challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. Polls remain inconclusive, but the race has drawn national attention as one of the few competitive seats in a state that typically votes reliably Republican in federal elections.

The contest became more complicated this week after former Vice President Kamala Harris sent an unsolicited fundraising email on Peltola's behalf, with half of the proceeds directed to Harris's own political organization. Peltola publicly rejected Harris's support, a calculated move in a state where Harris lost by 13 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. The episode highlights the challenge Democrats face in red-leaning states, where national party figures can be liabilities rather than assets for down-ballot candidates.

Republicans are watching the race closely as they seek to protect their Senate majority, while Democrats see Peltola — who previously held Alaska's at-large House seat — as one of their strongest candidates in a difficult environment. The race is seen as a bellwether for whether Democrats can compete in traditionally Republican territory by running candidates who actively distance themselves from national party leadership.
